Gnashing
năsh'ĭng
n. and part. (a grinding of the teeth in rage or anguish; rendering Greek brugmos and Hebrew charaq)
Middle English gnasten, of Scandinavian origin, imitative of the grinding of teeth. The Greek brugmos is likewise a sound-word: the grating of teeth.

Biblical Definition

The phrase “weeping and gnashing of teeth” is the Lord's own recurring description of the final state of the lost, and He uses it seven times — six in Matthew and once in Luke. It falls on the children of the kingdom cast into outer darkness (Mat 8:12); on those gathered out of the field at the end of the world and cast into the furnace of fire (Mat 13:42, 13:50); on the man without a wedding garment, bound hand and foot (Mat 22:13); on the servant cut asunder and appointed his portion with the hypocrites (Mat 24:51); on the unprofitable servant who buried his talent (Mat 25:30). Two things belong to the sound. Weeping is grief; gnashing, in its Old Testament use, is rage — the enemies of the righteous gnash upon him with their teeth (Psa 35:16; Lam 2:16), and the council gnashed on Stephen with their teeth before they stoned him (Act 7:54). Hell is therefore not portrayed as sorrowful repentance. It is grief and fury together, and unending. That the tenderest Teacher who ever spoke is the one who says it seven times is a fact the church is not at liberty to soften.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines gnashing as a grinding or striking of the teeth together, as in rage, pain, or despair.

expand to see more

GNASH, v.t. To strike the teeth together, as in anger or pain.

GNASH, v.i. To grind the teeth; to rage even to collision of the teeth.

GNASHING, n. A grinding or striking of the teeth in rage or anguish.

Key Scripture

Mat 8:12 — "But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth."

Mat 25:30 — "And cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth."

Psa 112:10 — "The wicked shall see it, and be grieved; he shall gnash with his teeth, and melt away: the desire of the wicked shall perish."

Modern Corruption

Annihilationism and universalism both require the gnashing to stop, and both must therefore explain away the one description of hell that Christ Himself repeated most often.

expand to see more

The doctrine of eternal conscious punishment is not built on a single proof text; it is built on the settled speech of Christ, and this phrase is its signature. Seven times He said weeping and gnashing of teeth, and He said it in the plainest didactic settings — the sermon, the parables of the kingdom, the discourse on the last things. Annihilationism, argued in the evangelical world by Edward Fudge and John Stott among others, must read the fire as consuming rather than tormenting and the gnashing as brief; universalism, in its ancient Origenist and modern forms, must read it as remedial. Both proposals founder on the same rock: the gnashing is rage, not repentance. In every Old Testament use — the enemies gnashing on the righteous in Psalm 35, the adversaries hissing and gnashing in Lamentations 2, the council gnashing on Stephen in Acts 7 — teeth are ground in fury against God or His servants. Nothing in the picture is turning toward God. The LBCF (32.2) confesses the wicked cast into eternal torments and punished with everlasting destruction, and the confession is only saying after Him what the Lord Jesus said first. The dictionary preaches the doctrine as He preached it: soberly, often, and with tears — never with relish, and never with revision.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek brugmos (G1030), a grating or gnashing of the teeth; brucho (G1031), to grind the teeth; Hebrew charaq (H2786), to grind or gnash the teeth in rage.

expand to see more

Greek brugmos (G1030) — a gnashing, a grating of the teeth; always joined to weeping and always in the Lord's own words about judgment; Matthew 8:12, 13:42, 22:13, 25:30.

Greek brucho (G1031) — to grind the teeth; used once, of the Sanhedrin against Stephen; Acts 7:54.

Hebrew charaq (H2786) — to grind or gnash the teeth in rage; the enemies of the righteous, and the wicked who melts away; Psalm 35:16, 112:10, Lamentations 2:16.

Usage

"“There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” — seven times from the lips of Christ."

"“He shall gnash with his teeth, and melt away” — the rage of the wicked at the prosperity of the righteous."

"“They gnashed on him with their teeth” — the council before the stoning of Stephen."
